An offender who has failed to completely pay off £690 in court fines since September, 2014, claimed he had totally forgotten and it had completely slipped his mind.
Chesterfield magistrates’ court heard on December 5 how Graham John Roberts, 29, of Manvers Road, Calow, Chesterfield, owed the court money after committing criminal damage and he also had a subsequent conviction for being drunk-and-disorderly from December 2014.
Roberts had been paying £30 a week and £330 had been paid leaving an outstanding £360 and a warrant had to be issued for his arrest.
He told the court: “I totally forgot about it. It completely passed my mind.”
Roberts added that he had been struggling because he was unemployed but he has since found work.
Magistrates ordered Roberts to pay £100 immediately and subsequently he must pay £30 a week.
Roberts was warned that people who allow fines payments to escalate and fail to pay can face custodial sentences.

He explained to the magistrates that the matter had slipped his memory and acknowledged past difficulties due to unemployment, though he is now employed. Ryan Sipes is making good on a new tag—Mr. Versatility. He debuted in American Flat Track last weekend by logging the fastest qualifying time in the Singles Class at the Springfield TT. A crash in the main left him tenth at the finish. A few days later, he was named as a member of Team USA for this year's International Six-Days Enduro. Sipes won that event overall in 2015.
Last year, Ryan showed up at the Thunder Valley National on a 125 two-stroke and won the 125 Dream Race. So we asked him about his experience in flat track, and also threw in a question about racing at elevation. Sounds like it impacts the bikes much more than the riders. Go, Ryan, go!
1. How did the Springfield Flat Track TT go?
Sipes: Man, I had a blast! Results-wise, it could have been better if I hadn’t crashed in the main, but considering it was just my seventh time riding flat track, I’m not too mad about it. I qualified fastest out of practice, which was a huge surprise to me. I got first gate pick in the heat race, but then jumped the light! (D’oh!) So I started last on the restart, but made some passes and got into the semi. I got fifth there, which put me on the second row for the main. My bike is super fast, so I got a great jump and was actually third going into the second corner, but then somebody got landed on behind me and they red-flagged it. On the restart I came out sixth, made the pass for fifth, and felt like I could maybe get on the podium until I slid out in turn one. I got up last and passed a bunch of dudes to get up to tenth. Like I said, it would have been better if I hadn’t crashed, but I had a freakin’ blast. Flat track is super fun. Huge shoutout to my buddy JD Beach for helping me out on race day and all the riding tips. He was a huge help!

IT’S not quite an Oscar, more an Oscar plaque, but Adelaide software engineer Vikas Sathaye was honoured last month for helping to develop an aerial camera mount used in Hollywood blockbusters.
Mr Sathaye, 50, in 2009 joined Shotover Camera Systems in New Zealand where he and three colleagues developed a steadycam helicopter mount that was so successful the crew of Walking With Dinosaurs wanted the prototype.
Camera Icon Vikas Sathaye and wife Ashwini with his mini-Oscar. AAP/ Keryn Stevens Picture: News Limited
“They had a very tight schedule and they wanted us to fit their cameras and lenses to our 3D prototype gimbal (mount),” Mr Sathaye, who grew up in Mumbai, said.
Weight problems were solved and the K1 camera was picked up by other Hollywood films needing judder-free helicopter footage, among them Dunkirk, Guardians of the Galaxy Vol 2 and The Revenant.
The camera earned the Scientific and Engineering Award from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in Los Angeles last month.
Mr Sathaye — who moved to Adelaide in 2012 and works with RFI Technology Solutions to develop wireless software for emergency services — accepted the mini Oscar watched by wife Ashwini and daughter Tanvi, 19, now in her second year of software engineering at the University of Adelaide.
“She was inspired and said she wanted to do something similar to her father — that was really very joyful for my wife and myself, that our daughter was also interested,” he said.
rewrite:
While it may not be the iconic golden statuette, Adelaide software engineer Vikas Sathaye recently received a prestigious Oscar plaque from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. The honor, bestowed last month, recognized his contribution to creating an advanced aerial camera stabilization system utilized in major film productions.

Sathaye, aged 50, began working with New Zealand's Shotover Camera Systems in 2009. There, he collaborated with three others to engineer a helicopter-mounted steadycam device. Their prototype proved so effective that the production team for *Walking With Dinosaurs* urgently requested it for their project. Sathaye, originally from Mumbai, explained that the crew needed to attach their specific cameras and lenses to the new 3D gimbal mount within a constrained timeframe.

After resolving initial weight challenges, the resulting K1 camera system was adopted by numerous Hollywood studios seeking perfectly smooth footage from helicopters. It has since been used in acclaimed films such as *Dunkirk*, *Guardians of the Galaxy Vol 2*, and *The Revenant*.

Now residing in Adelaide since 2012, Sathaye develops wireless software for emergency responders at RFI Technology Solutions. He accepted the miniature Oscar accolade alongside his wife, Ashwini, and their 19-year-old daughter, Tanvi, who is currently pursuing a software engineering degree at the University of Adelaide. He expressed profound happiness that his daughter felt inspired by his achievement and aspires to follow a similar innovative path.

Tom Izzo is not one to beat around the bush. He often takes blame for the Michigan State Spartans’ mistakes and struggles and calls it like he sees it.
So when the head coach found out ESPN commentator Dan Dakich insulted the Spartans’ fan base and the school’s education quality, he went on an uncensored rant.
In a since-deleted tweet, Dakich – whose son, Andrew, is a senior guard for the Michigan Wolverines – said “Sparty not only whines but now just dumb!! Couldn’t get into UM??” In more Twitter exchanges, he repeatedly called MSU fans whiners.
@sportz5176 @budrowley that's great but sweetheart nobody whines like Sparty!!! — Dan Dakich (@dandakich) February 8, 2017
And that led to MSU’s Izzone student section chanting, “We hate Dakich” throughout the Spartans’ 74-66 win over Ohio State on Tuesday – a game he was calling for ESPN.
When Izzo got some context for the chants, he went off.
Via the Detroit Free Press:
“If I would have known that before the game, I would have embarrassed myself almost as much as he embarrassed himself, and I would have led the chants,” Izzo said, his voice slightly cracking. “Because calling us whiners and that is kind of unprofessional. Classy broadcasters, like George Blaha and everybody else, wouldn’t have even thought to do something like that on TV. But saying our students couldn’t get in there? And he’s doing games for Michigan when his son is there? That is a disappointment, and that is ridiculous. “And I think it’s funny because I got no respect for him for that. And I am going to publicly say it – you can tweet it, you can read it, you can do whatever you want with it – but Twitter got him in trouble, and he earned it. I am surprised ESPN would let somebody say something like that, that works for them.”
He also added that he “would have loved” to join the Izzone in chanting and said he owes MSU fans and students an apology – but acknowleded he probably won’t get it.
rewrite:
Tom Izzo is known for his directness. The Michigan State coach typically accepts responsibility for his team's errors and challenges, and he speaks with unfiltered honesty. Therefore, when he learned that ESPN analyst Dan Dakich had disparaged both the Spartan fan community and the academic standards of the university, Izzo launched into a frank and impassioned critique.

Dakich, whose son plays for the rival Michigan Wolverines, posted a tweet—later removed—stating, “Sparty not only whines but now just dumb!! Couldn’t get into UM??” In subsequent social media interactions, he consistently labeled MSU supporters as complainers. This prompted the Izzone, Michigan State’s student section, to repeatedly chant “We hate Dakich” during the Spartans’ Tuesday victory over Ohio State, a game Dakich was broadcasting.

Upon understanding the reason for the chants, Izzo expressed his strong disapproval. He stated that had he been aware earlier, he would have joined the students in their vocal protest, even if it meant appearing undignified, because Dakich’s remarks were, in his view, deeply unprofessional. Izzo contrasted this behavior with that of respectful broadcasters like George Blaha, who would never make such comments on air.

He particularly objected to the insinuation that Michigan State students were not academically qualified for the University of Michigan, noting the clear conflict of interest given Dakich’s son’s enrollment there and Dakich’s role covering Michigan games. Izzo called the situation both disappointing and absurd, explicitly stating he lost all respect for the commentator. He added that Dakich’s troubles were self-inflicted through his social media activity and expressed surprise that ESPN would employ someone capable of such statements.

Izzo concluded by saying he would have enthusiastically participated in the chants and believes an apology is owed to the Michigan State community, though he doubts one will ever be forthcoming.

The 33% boost in fees will be matched by a contribution from Huron itself.
“Today, we are proud to announce that up to five student refugees, already arrived in Canada, will receive a full-tuition scholarship from Huron University College when they register,” Dr. Barry Craig, principal of Huron University College, said.

These actions align with our mission Barry Craig
The school’s second such decision this school year; In September, Huron offered $60,000 scholarships for students affected by the Trump administration’s decision to end legal protection to children of illegal U.S. immigrants, so-called Dreamers. FILE PHOTO: The seal of the Department of Commerce is pictured in Washington, D.C., U.S. March 10, 2017. REUTERS/Eric Thayer
WASHINGTON The U.S. Commerce Department is launching a new review of whether China should be treated as a market economy country, a designation that would effectively limit the calculation of anti-dumping duties on China-made goods.
Buried in a federal notice on Wednesday about an investigation into alleged dumping of Chinese aluminum foil into the U.S. market, the department said it is seeking public comments on China's non-market economy status.
The review comes as the White House prepares for the first face-to-face meeting between President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on April 6-7 at Trump's Mar-a-Lago retreat in Florida.
China's non-market economy status is considered an irritant for Beijing as the Trump administration works on trade policies aimed at reducing the flow of Chinese imports in to the United States.
When China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, its accession terms allowed other WTO members to treat it as a non-market economy and use a third country's prices to assess whether Chinese goods were being sold below cost.
But part of that clause expired on Dec. 11, 2016, which China says means WTO trading partners must drop their use of such surrogate pricing, which has led to higher U.S. anti-dumping duties on imported Chinese goods.
The United States and European Union failed to change their view of China's status. A day later, Beijing launched a formal complaint against them before the WTO.
The Commerce Department last conducted a review of China's non-market economy status in 2006, determining that China failed on all six determining criteria, which are:
* the extent to which the country's currency is convertible into other currencies;
* the extent to which wage rates are determined by free bargaining by labor and management;
* the extent to which joint ventures or other investments by foreign firms are permitted in the country;
* the extent of government ownership or control of the means of production;
* the extent of government control over allocation of resources and over price and output decisions of enterprises, and
* other factors the administering authority considers appropriate.
(Reporting by David Lawder, editing by G Crosse)
rewrite:
A photograph taken in Washington, D.C., on March 10, 2017, shows the official insignia of the U.S. Department of Commerce. The image is credited to Reuters photographer Eric Thayer.

In a development from Washington, the Commerce Department has initiated a fresh examination concerning China's classification as a market economy. Such a designation would significantly alter how anti-dumping tariffs on products from China are determined, typically resulting in lower duties. This inquiry was announced within a public notice related to a separate probe into suspected dumping of aluminum foil from China into American markets. The department is soliciting input from the public on whether China should still be considered a non-market economy.

This reassessment coincides with preparations for an upcoming summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, scheduled for early April at Trump's Florida estate, Mar-a-Lago. The issue of China's non-market label is a point of contention for Beijing, particularly as the current U.S. administration devises trade strategies intended to decrease the volume of Chinese imports.

Upon entering the World Trade Organization in 2001, China agreed to provisions permitting other member nations to classify it as a non-market economy for a transitional period. This allowed countries to use price data from a third-party nation to evaluate if Chinese exports were being sold at unfairly low prices. A segment of this agreement concluded in December 2016. Chinese officials argue this expiration obligates WTO partners, including the U.S. and European Union, to cease the surrogate pricing method, which has historically resulted in elevated anti-dumping duties on Chinese goods. Both the U.S. and EU have maintained their stance, prompting China to file a formal dispute with the WTO shortly after the deadline.

The Commerce Department previously evaluated China's economic status in 2006, concluding it did not meet any of the six established criteria for a market economy. These benchmarks assess factors such as currency convertibility, the degree of free wage negotiation, openness to foreign investment, state ownership of production assets, governmental influence over resource allocation and corporate pricing, along with any other relevant considerations determined by the authorities.

This report contains information from journalist David Lawder, with editorial contributions from G Crosse.

TORONTO — Ontario's premier said she'd welcome U.S. President Donald Trump's education secretary to visit the province's public schools if she chooses to reschedule a cancelled trip, even though she disagrees with some of Betsy DeVos' positions.
Kathleen Wynne said Friday that she was looking forward to an opportunity to show DeVos a strong, publicly funded education system.
DeVos cancelled a planned visit for Thursday and Friday this week just one day in advance, citing "scheduling issues," though the U.S. Department of Education noted the trip had merely been postponed.
The visit had caused some controversy in Ontario, where teachers' unions expressed concerns over DeVos' advocacy for school choice, including vouchers that allow kids to attend publicly funded but privately operated charter schools, or private schools on the public dime.
The NDP called on the government to not allow DeVos to tour schools in the province — a position Wynne said she doesn't understand.
"I don't agree with the positions that Secretary DeVos has taken in the past, that's true, but I think that's all the more reason to have an opportunity to showcase what we do in our schools and how strong a publicly funded education system can be," Wynne said Friday.
"So I honestly don't understand why we would want to hide that under a bushel. I would think we'd want to celebrate the success of our publicly funded education system."
DeVos has also attracted protests recently for revoking a guidance that instructed colleges on how to handle sexual assault cases, saying the previous policy was unfairly skewed against those accused of assault, and for the department of education rolling back rules allowing transgender students to use school restrooms of their choice.
Wynne has advocated for protections for LGBT Ontarians and her government launched a large campaign aimed at ending sexual harassment and violence.
Despite differences of opinion, Wynne said she would want to display Ontario's education system.
rewrite:
Ontario's Premier Kathleen Wynne expressed her willingness to host U.S. Education Secretary Betsy DeVos for a tour of the province's public schools, should the previously planned trip be rearranged. This openness persists despite Wynne's stated disagreements with several of DeVos's policy stances. Speaking on Friday, Wynne noted she viewed a potential visit as a chance to demonstrate the strengths of Ontario's robust, publicly funded approach to education.

DeVos cancelled her scheduled two-day visit on short notice, with the U.S. Department of Education describing the postponement as due to scheduling conflicts. The planned trip had already sparked debate within Ontario, particularly among teachers' unions. Their concerns centered on DeVos's promotion of "school choice" models, such as voucher programs that direct public funds toward charter or private institutions.

The provincial New Democratic Party had urged the government to deny DeVos access to schools, a stance Wynne explicitly rejected. She argued that differing viewpoints make it more, not less, important to present Ontario's system. Wynne questioned why the province would conceal its achievements, suggesting instead that its successful public education model should be proudly highlighted.

DeVos has recently faced criticism for other actions, including rescinding federal guidelines on campus sexual assault investigations, which she deemed unfair to the accused. Her department has also reversed protections permitting transgender students to use bathrooms aligning with their gender identity. Authorities Looking for 'Mystery Woman' Seen With Las Vegas Gunman
The Las Vegas massacre has led to many Democratic lawmakers and liberals pushing for stricter gun control legislation.
Larry O'Connor, a radio host and Mediaite contributing editor, wrote a recent piece pointing out that many on the left declare the U.S. government to be evil and racist, while simultaneously arguing that evil and racist government should determine who can and cannot arm themselves.
"I don't know about you, but if a hurricane comes or some other natural disaster and the government actually can't do anything or won't do anything to help me, I'd like to have a gun around at my disposal," O'Connor said on "Tucker Carlson Tonight."
Carlson pointed out that no matter when or where a mass shooting occurs, Democratic lawmakers default to blaming Middle America and the Second Amendment.
O'Connor suggested it's no coincidence that they try and blame the people who put President Trump in the White House.
"For how many months have we been told Donald Trump is a fascist, he's this century's Adolf Hitler?" O'Connor said. "Now, if our Democratic republic is so fragile that Adolf Hitler could become our president, my God, why would we not want to be able to arm ourselves?"
"And why would we want 'Adolf Hitler' to be the one who decides who gets a gun and who doesn't?" he continued. "We've seen that story play out. It's not a good one."
Watch more above.
Dana Loesch: Monsters Exist and Millions of Americans Want to Protect Themselves

The Chicago woman who live streamed the racially charged beating of a white Chicago teen with mental disabilities, pleaded guilty to hate crimes and was sentenced to just 4 years probation this Friday.
Brittany Covington, 19, has been in custody since her arrest in January.
Cook County Circuit Judge William Hooks called the event “horrific” and banned Covington from using social media for her 4 years of probation. Covington was also banned from communicating with the other two co-defendants, and she has been ordered 200 hours of community service.
Hooks told Covington he could have imposed a prison sentence but added, “I’m not sure if I did that you’d be coming out any better.”
I disagree, and I’m sure the parents of that disabled child, and other families would agree. This disabled child was lured from school to an empty apartment where he could be tied up and brutalized on camera just because he was white, this certainly calls for jail time. This 19 year old girl should not be allowed back in society if this is the type of damage she is capable of causing.
She clearly wasn’t thinking about the repercussions of her actions in the slightest if she was live streaming the crime on Facebook, which is scary, a young woman who is willing to commit a crime this heinous should be removed from society until she can learn to live with others.
Three others were charged in the incident: alleged ringleader Jordan Hill, 19, as well as Tesfaye Cooper, 19, and Covington’s sister, Tanishia, 25. Their cases are still pending.
All of these young adults deserve to spend time behind bars for this disgusting act of violence and racism. There is clearly a deep seeded anger here for the white population that isn’t going to be solved with 4 years off Facebook, these young adults need help, and need to be removed from society.
rewrite:
A Chicago resident received a sentence of four years' probation after admitting to hate crimes for broadcasting the assault of a mentally disabled white teenager, an attack motivated by racial animus. Brittany Covington, aged 19, has been detained since January following her involvement.

In court, Cook County Circuit Judge William Hooks described the incident as "horrific." As conditions of her probation, Covington is prohibited from using social media and from contacting two other defendants linked to the case. She must also complete 200 hours of community service. Judge Hooks remarked that while he could have sentenced her to imprisonment, he was uncertain incarceration would lead to her rehabilitation.

However, a different perspective holds that probation is an insufficient consequence. The victim, a disabled minor, was deliberately taken from school to a vacant residence, where he was restrained and violently assaulted while the event was recorded, targeted solely because of his race. Such deliberate cruelty warrants a prison sentence. A person capable of orchestrating and broadcasting such brutality poses a danger to the community and should not be reintegrated into society without meaningful intervention.

The decision to livestream the crime on Facebook demonstrates a profound disregard for the consequences, indicating a disturbing mindset. An individual willing to commit an act of such malice requires isolation from society until they can demonstrate a capacity for peaceful coexistence.

Three additional individuals—Jordan Hill, 19, identified as the alleged leader, Tesfaye Cooper, 19, and Tanishia Covington, 25—face charges related to the event, with their cases ongoing. All those involved deserve substantial prison time for this abhorrent racist violence. The profound racial hostility evident in this crime cannot be addressed merely through restricted internet access. These individuals require serious intervention and must be separated from society to ensure public safety and accountability.

JOHANNESBURG - Growthpoint Properties, the largest South African real estate investment trust (Reit) listed on the JSE with assets on three continents, has established a dedicated trading and development business unit.
Estienne de Klerk, the chief executive of Growthpoint South Africa, said yesterday that the new specialised division would play a key role in creating excellent business opportunities for the company and world-class premises for its clients.
Until now, Growthpoint’s in-house trading and development skills were held within each sector of the company’s portfolio, including office, retail and industrial. The new business unit would combine and integrate Growthpoint’s cross-sector development and trading expertise to optimise its business strengths.
De Klerk said the new business unit would enable Growthpoint to provide their clients with an extra service that met their needs. “Besides providing existing buildings, we can create new buildings for them that meet their very specific, bespoke requirements.”
De Klerk added that Growthpoint’s trading and development team was a key part of their business and had played a significant role in building the company’s portfolio. He said Growthpoint’s goal was to generate consistent, recurring income from third-party development fees and trading profit that totalled no more than 1percent to 2percent of its distributable income.
Rudolf Pienaar, the new chief investment and development officer at Growthpoint, said development played a key role in Growthpoint’s South African investment strategy with tailor-made assets designed to enhance its portfolio and retain and attract quality clients.
However, Pienaar said that in working closely with its clients Growthpoint had found that some of their needs went beyond a simple tenancy. He said their company policy may require them to own certain types of properties; they might need to dispose of a property asset to become a tenant of Growthpoint, or they could require specialised premises that could only be custom-developed.
- BUSINESS REPORT
rewrite:
JOHANNESBURG – Growthpoint Properties, South Africa’s biggest JSE-listed real estate investment trust (Reit) with holdings across three global regions, has formed a new, focused division for trading and development activities.

Estienne de Klerk, Growthpoint South Africa’s CEO, announced that this specialized unit will be instrumental in unlocking valuable prospects for the firm and delivering top-tier facilities to its customers.

Previously, Growthpoint’s capabilities in trading and development were dispersed across different segments of its holdings, such as office, retail, and industrial properties. The newly established unit will bring together and unify the company’s expertise in development and trading from all sectors, aiming to maximize its commercial advantages.

De Klerk explained that this move allows Growthpoint to offer clients an additional, tailored service. “Rather than only supplying current buildings, we can now design and construct new properties that fit their unique, customized demands,” he noted.

He also emphasized that the trading and development team has been central to Growthpoint’s operations and has greatly contributed to expanding its asset base. The company’s objective, he said, is to produce steady, repeat earnings from external development fees and trading gains, which should account for up to 1% to 2% of its distributable income.

Rudolf Pienaar, Growthpoint’s recently appointed chief investment and development officer, stated that development is a crucial element of the company’s investment approach in South Africa. Custom-built properties are intended to improve its portfolio and help keep and draw high-caliber clients.

Pienaar added, however, that through close collaboration with clients, Growthpoint has recognized that some requirements extend beyond basic leasing arrangements. Corporate guidelines might obligate them to hold particular kinds of real estate; they may need to sell an owned property to become a Growthpoint tenant, or they could seek highly specialized spaces that must be developed from the ground up.

By Charles Kumolu
IRKED by the poor power supply in the country, the Nigerian Young Professionals Forum, NYPF, has concluded plans to hold a two-day workshop for host community youth leaders where power stations and pipeline installations are located across the country.
A statement by the convener of the event, scheduled to hold from September 25 to 26 in Abuja, NYPF, Mr. Moses Siasia, said the move became important given the need to engage key actors in the sabotage of the power sector, who had contributed to Nigeria’s less than 3,000 megawatts generating status.
His words: “This shameful act of sabotage is mainly caused by youths of our generation, who have lost faith and do not see themselves as stakeholders in our society.
“It is imperative to note with our recent findings that it is only few stakeholders and players in the power sector that is concerned about finding a solution to this menace, while some see it as a cash cow because of their selfish interests.
“But for us as NYPF, we see it as an opportunity to contribute our quota towards nation building. At the end of the workshop, participants will be strategically engaged as volunteers for proper security of the nation’s power assets for effective and efficient increased power supply and service delivery.”
rewrite:

Recent investigations reveal that only a limited number of power sector participants are genuinely committed to resolving this issue, while others exploit it for personal profit. The NYPF, however, views this as a chance to support national development. Russian Olympic Committee President Alexander Zhukov has praised the performances of the 19 athletes from his country who competed as neutrals at the International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) World Championships here.
Russians were forced to take part under the Authorised Neutral Athletes (ANA) banner because country has been banned from international competition by the IAAF since November 2015 following allegations of state-supported doping.
The team won a total of six medals to finish ninth in the overall medals table, finishing ahead of Germany, Australia and Jamaica.
Russian athletes actually won more medals competing as ANA than they did at the previous World Championships in Beijing two years ago when, under their own flag, they collected four.
Their medals total at London was made up of one gold and five silver.
The gold medal was won by Mariya Lasitskene in the high jump, successfully defending the title she won had won in Beijing in 2015 under her maiden name Kuchina.
"One gold and five silver medals," Zhukov told Russia's official state news agency TASS.
"Half of the team could count on medals."
Zhukov added: "Under such conditions, these are remarkable results."
"I believe that, if we take the overall psychological factor, the fact that we have not won medals at international competitions for a long time, that most of the athletes came without their coaches, and that does make an impact, they performed very well.
"I want to congratulate all our athletes."
Besides Lasitskene, other Russians to win medals at London included Danil Lysenko.
He won a silver medal during the final session last night in the men's high jump.
Other silver medals were won by Sergey Shubenkov in the 110 metres hurdles, Darya Klishina in the women's long jump, Valeriy Pronkin in the men's hammer throw and Sergei Shirokobokov in the men's 20 kilometres walk.
rewrite:
Alexander Zhukov, who leads the Russian Olympic Committee, has commended the nineteen Russian competitors who participated under a neutral designation at the recent IAAF World Championships. These athletes were required to compete as Authorised Neutral Athletes due to an ongoing suspension of Russia’s track and field federation by the IAAF, a penalty imposed in late 2015 over accusations of government-backed doping.

The neutral contingent secured six medals in total, earning ninth place in the overall standings and outperforming nations such as Germany, Australia, and Jamaica. This medal count surpassed Russia’s performance at the prior World Championships in Beijing, where the team, competing under its national flag, obtained four medals. In London, the haul consisted of one gold and five silver medals.

Mariya Lasitskene claimed the sole gold by winning the women’s high jump, thereby repeating her 2015 victory from Beijing, where she competed under her former surname, Kuchina. Zhukov, in remarks to the Russian news agency TASS, highlighted the achievement of one gold and five silvers, noting that approximately half of the team members were in contention for podium finishes. He described the outcomes as exceptional given the difficult circumstances.

Zhukov pointed to the significant psychological challenge of returning to international competition after a prolonged absence from medal contention, further complicated by many athletes being without their personal coaches. Despite these obstacles, he stated that the team performed admirably and extended his congratulations to all participants.

Additional medalists for the neutral Russian group included Danil Lysenko, who earned silver in the men’s high jump during the final day of competition. Further silver medals were awarded to Sergey Shubenkov in the 110-meter hurdles, Darya Klishina in the women’s long jump, Valeriy Pronkin in the men’s hammer throw, and Sergei Shirokobokov in the men’s 20-kilometer race walk.

Joey Badass, who’s got a busy summer ahead of him as he kicks off his Amerikkkana Tour alongside Compton rappers Buddy and Boogie, has announced the date of the 4th annual Steez Day Music Festival at Central Park’s Summerstage in New York City featuring Joey himself along with his crew Pro Era, as well as fellow Beast Coast crew members Flatbush Zombies and The Underachievers, and affiliated Brooklyn MC Stro.
Steez Day Festival is just one festival that has been started in honor of a fallen up-and-coming rap luminary by his surviving crew mates, with ASAP Mob following in Pro Era’s footsteps with their own Yams Day. Unfortunately, the 2017 Yams Day Festival was shut down due to attendees brawling.
Hopefully, Steez Day won’t be marred by bellicose fans, as it’s meant to be a celebration of the life of Pro Era and Beast Coast member Capital Steez, who committed suicide on Christmas Eve in 2012, sending shockwaves through New York’s then-burgeoning next-wave underground rap scene. It was Steez who initially coined the name for the extended crew including The Underachievers and Flatbush Zombies, and was known for his precocious, socially conscious lyrics.
Unfortunately, Steez wasn’t around to witness the eventual success of his crew members, as Joey’s album All-Amerikkkan Badass rewrote the book on throwback, lyrical rap and Flatbush Zombies’ new album Vacation In Hell constituted a rip-roaring comeback for a crew that had been relatively quiet for a few years.
The 4th annual Steez Day 2018 will take over Central Park July 8. Tickets will be available this Friday, April 27.

This festival belongs to a category of tributes created by peers to remember a promising artist lost too soon. Similarly, the ASAP Mob organizes Yams Day, though its 2017 iteration was canceled following attendee violence.

The hope is that Steez Day remains peaceful, as it honors Capital Steez—a Pro Era and Beast Coast member who took his own life on Christmas Eve 2012. His death deeply affected New York's emerging underground rap community at the time. Steez is credited with naming the broader Beast Coast collective and was recognized for his mature, socially aware songwriting.

Tragically, he did not live to see his friends achieve later acclaim. Joey Badass’s album *All-Amerikkkan Badass* revitalized thoughtful, classic-style rap, while Flatbush Zombies’ record *Vacation In Hell* marked a vigorous return after a period of quiet.

The 2018 Steez Day festival is scheduled for July 8 in Central Park. Tickets go on sale Friday, April 27.

“Friday’s news of Apple’s permit to test self-driving cars in California should not have come as much of a surprise given the poorly kept secret of Project Titan,” Gene Munster writes for Loup Ventures. “But the permit begs the question of whether Apple is building a car or just building software for a car.”
“In an ideal world, Apple’s car project would involve the company building the actual automobile, combining hardware and software,” Munster writes. “In reality, the complexity of designing and manufacturing a vehicle may push the company to integrate deeply with an automotive partner or partners in an effort more similar to the Apple TV — plugging Apple’s technology into an existing product.”
“Apple is almost certainly exploring how it could build an entire car, but as we learned the hard way with an Apple television, exploration does not mean a product comes to market,” Munster writes. “Apple is the best connected device maker in the world and the car is the biggest connected device in the world.”
Read more in the full article here.
rewrite:
According to Gene Munster of Loup Ventures, Apple's recent authorization to trial autonomous vehicles in California was widely anticipated, largely due to the longstanding rumors surrounding its Project Titan. However, this development raises a critical uncertainty: is Apple's goal to manufacture a complete vehicle, or is it focused solely on creating the software that would operate it?

Munster suggests the optimal scenario would see Apple producing the entire car, merging its own hardware and software. Yet he acknowledges the immense difficulties of vehicle design and production. This could instead lead Apple to form a profound collaboration with one or more established automakers. Such a partnership might resemble its approach with Apple TV, where its technology is incorporated into a platform built by another company.

While Apple is undoubtedly investigating the possibility of building a car, Munster cautions that such research does not guarantee a market-ready product, a lesson learned from its television explorations. He concludes by noting the logical connection: Apple is the premier creator of internet-connected devices, and the modern automobile represents the most significant connected device available.

The Boss is Broadway bound.
Bruce Springsteen will make his Broadway debut at the Walter Kerr Theatre for an eight-week run in the fall, The Post has learned exclusively.
Sources say Springsteen will do a pared-down version of the set he usually performs in huge arenas and stadiums all over the world.
“He wants to play a smaller house,” a theater source says. “He wants to try something more intimate, and he likes the idea of being on Broadway.”
Dates haven’t been finalized, but Springsteen will likely open in November. He’ll perform five times a week. Jujamcyn Theaters, which owns the Kerr, gave him a sweetheart deal he couldn’t refuse: no rent for the eight weeks.
The 975-seat Kerr has been empty since the musical “Amélie” closed in May.
“He’ll keep the lights on in the building, and they’ll sell gazillions of dollars worth of booze,” a source says.
Springsteen will sell out the run in a minute, though whatever he makes will pale in comparison to the tens of millions of dollars he makes on tour.
But as one music source says: “He’s got all the money in the world. He can do what he likes.”
Some insiders believe Springsteen’s Broadway gig may be a curtain raiser to another project — turning his best-selling memoir, “Born To Run,” into a musical. Several producers, dollar signs dancing in their eyes, approached Springsteen about adapting the book for the stage after The Post reported he was interested in the idea.
It could be a blockbuster along the lines of “Jersey Boys” and “Beautiful: the Carole King Musical.”
But that’s a long way off. In the meantime, you’ll be able to see the Boss “live and in person” at the Kerr this fall.

The Walter Kerr, with 975 seats, has been vacant since the closure of "Amélie" last May. An anonymous source commented that Springsteen's presence will generate significant activity and concession revenue for the venue.

Tickets for the limited run are expected to sell out almost instantly. However, the earnings from this venture will be modest compared to the enormous revenues from his stadium tours. As one music industry observer remarked, financial gain is not the objective, as Springsteen has the freedom to pursue any artistic endeavor he chooses.

Such a production could potentially achieve major success, similar to other hit biographical musicals. That prospect, however, remains in the future. For now, audiences will have the opportunity to see Springsteen perform live at the Walter Kerr Theatre in the coming season.

Tom Brady will be sidelined Super Bowl Sunday.
“It’s my day off,” the 22-year-old Staten Island pizza deliveryman told The Post.
The die-hard Jets fan will spend the day rooting hard against his namesake instead.
“Enough is enough. … The Patriots win too many Super Bowls.”
Brady is just one of 31 Tom Bradys living in New York City, with at least one in every borough.
You’re most likely to bump and run into a Tom Brady in Brooklyn, where 11 reside. There are five in the Bronx, four on Staten Island and two in Queens. There are nine listed in Manhattan, including the one married to Brazilian supermodel Gisele Bundchen and living in a $14 million apartment at One Madison in the Flatiron District.
Like the pretty boy quarterback, Staten Island Tom Brady’s father is of Irish descent, while his mom has Polish roots.
“I even have his middle name — Edward. It’s a curse and it’s a blessing,” said Brady.
“Every time I meet new people they say, ‘Are you related to Tom Brady?’ I’ve messed around with a couple of people and said, ‘Yeah, I’m his nephew.’ Some people fall for it,” he laughed.
Staten Island Tom, who cuts lawns in the summer, doesn’t have the NFL superstar’s $180 million net worth, but he does have his confidence.
“Tell Gisele if she ever gets tired … I’m 6-2 and single,” he quipped.
Tom Brady from Queens is no lookalike. The 69-year-old tour bus driver, at 5-foot-9 and 260 pounds, is built more for the couch than the gridiron.
“I’m Tom Brady and I have air in my footballs,” he joked.
He’s even driven the Patriots around town but can’t recall if his namesake was aboard his bus because “I don’t have any interest in football.”
For Eagles fans keeping score, there are zero Nick Foles listed in the city.

universities in Leeds have made almost £400,000 from fining students for overdue library books in the past three years.
Leeds University accrued the most money from overdue books, collecting more than £211,000 in fines since the 2014/2015 academic year.
Leeds Beckett, which collected £147,509, was the second highest, while Leeds Trinity University was third with fines totalling £27,682
A spokesperson for the University of Leeds said: “The university has five libraries and nearly 33,000 students, so our size is a factor in any comparison of library fines, and all fines are invested back into our libraries.”
With fines as little as 10p a day for each day a book is overdue, it shows that students are returning thousands of books late each year.
The universities say that all the fines are ploughed back into library services, with money spent on resources, including books and journals, “that it is benefited directly by the student”.
A spokesperson for Leeds Beckett University said: “Fines are used as a strategy to ensure the prompt return of books and to maximise book availability for all students in a context of sharing resources. Staff are also charged fines at the same level.
“Students generally support the use of fines to encourage their fellow students to bring back books promptly so they all get a chance to use them.”
Students at the University of Leeds only start incurring fines if the borrowed book has been requested by someone else, and they must then fork out £2.50 per day if the item is overdue.
A Leeds University Union spokesperson said: “The cost of student living is an ongoing conversation between us and the university. We will continue to work with the libraries to ensure that students are kept well informed on policies and procedures that may lead to fines and that these are fair and transparent.”

A Ventura backpacker missing for more than a day in Los Padres National Forest northeast of Lake Cachuma was rescued Saturday night by a Santa Barbara County Sheriff’s Department helicopter and the all-volunteer Sheriff’s Search and Rescue Team.
Sheriff’s Department spokesman Drew Sugars said Sunday that the 25-year-old Ventura man and three friends had set out Wednesday from the Upper Oso/Paradise Road area, about 10 miles north of Santa Barbara. The group was 12-15 miles into a trek in the Mission Pine Basin area when the man became separated from the group around midday Friday, he said.
When the man failed to appear Saturday morning, Sugars said, the three other backpackers hiked out and called 9-1-1 to report him missing.
The Search and Rescue Team and the Sheriff’s Aviation Unit were deployed around 5:30 p.m. Saturday, Sugars said.
Just before 7 p.m. Saturday, the crew of sheriff’s Copter One located the missing hiker near the trail between Upper Oso and Mission Pine Basin, Sugars said. The helicopter landed to pick him up, then transported him Upper Oso Campground, where a Search and Rescue unit was waiting.
Sugars said the man was dehydrated and exhausted, and he was treated at the scene by a crew from American Medical Response. The hiker’s identity was not released.

According to Sheriff’s Department spokesperson Drew Sugars, the 25-year-old man and three companions began their hike on Wednesday from the Upper Oso and Paradise Road vicinity, roughly ten miles north of Santa Barbara. The group had traveled between twelve and fifteen miles into the Mission Pine Basin region when the individual became separated from the others around noon on Friday.

After the missing man did not return by Saturday morning, his fellow hikers exited the trail and contacted emergency services to report his disappearance. The Search and Rescue Team and the Sheriff’s Aviation Unit were dispatched at approximately 5:30 p.m. on Saturday.

Shortly before 7 p.m., the crew of the sheriff’s helicopter, Copter One, spotted the lost hiker close to the path connecting Upper Oso and Mission Pine Basin. The aircraft landed to retrieve him and then flew him to Upper Oso Campground, where a ground team from Search and Rescue was stationed.

Sugars reported that the hiker was suffering from dehydration and extreme fatigue. He received medical attention at the site from American Medical Response personnel. The identity of the rescued individual was not disclosed.

The loss of forests in Africa in the past century is substantially less than previously estimated, an analysis of historical records and paleontology evidence by Yale researchers shows.
Previous estimates put deforestation at 35% to 55% on the continent since 1900. The new analysis estimates closed-canopy forests have shrunk by 21.7%, according to findings published Dec. 11 in the journal Nature Ecology and Evolution. However, research also shows that some West and East African forests have been reduced between 80% and 90%.
Earlier surveys incorrectly labelled ancient savannas as newly deforested regions, said A. Carla Staver, assistant professor of ecology and evolutionary biology and senior author of the study.
The new analysis should help focus conservation efforts in Africa, she said.
"There is a global effort to increase the number of trees that can trap carbon," Staver said. "In Africa, it would make the most sense to focus these efforts in areas that have truly been deforested rather than in areas which have long been savannas."
Staver and former Yale postdoc Julie C. Aleman, now at the University of Montreal, used traditional sources such as early 20th-century European maps to estimate the extent of African forests in 1900. But the team also cross-checked the documents with paleontological records -- including pollen, leaf parts known as phytoliths, and charcoal preserved in lake sediment and soil -- to reconstruct the historical ecology of tropical regions of Africa.
The single greatest contributor to continental deforestation was conversion of forests in West African countries including Ghana and Sierra Leone. However, the team also found that forests had actually expanded in Central African countries such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Central African Republic.
"As conservationists, it is easy to look at this study as good news -- that deforestation isn't as bad as we thought," Staver said. "The bad news is that central African forests have been spared because violent conflicts have prevented economic development, at the costs of human lives and livelihoods."
###
Aleman is lead author of the study and Yale's Mart Jarzyna is a co-author.
The research was funded by the National Science Foundation, the Seessel Fund, and the Yale Climate and Energy Institute.
rewrite:
A recent study from Yale University, examining historical documents and paleontological data, reveals that the reduction of Africa's forest cover over the last hundred years is not as severe as earlier assessments had concluded.

Earlier approximations suggested that between 35% and 55% of the continent's forests had been lost since 1900. In contrast, this new research, published in *Nature Ecology & Evolution*, indicates a decline of approximately 21.7% for dense, closed-canopy forests. It does note, however, that certain forests in West and East Africa have suffered losses reaching 80 to 90 percent.

According to senior author A. Carla Staver, an assistant professor of ecology and evolutionary biology, prior inaccuracies stemmed from misclassifying ancient savannas as recently cleared forest land. This refined understanding, she says, can help direct conservation resources more effectively across the continent.

Staver notes a worldwide initiative to plant more trees for carbon sequestration. For Africa, she emphasizes that such projects should prioritize lands that have actually experienced forest loss, rather than areas that have historically been grasslands.

To gauge the historical extent of forests around 1900, Staver and lead author Julie C. Aleman, a former Yale postdoctoral researcher now at the University of Montreal, consulted sources like colonial-era maps. They supplemented these records with paleontological evidence—such as ancient pollen, microscopic plant silica particles called phytoliths, and charcoal deposits found in lake beds and soils—to build a more reliable picture of Africa's past ecological landscape.

The most significant forest loss occurred in West African nations like Ghana and Sierra Leone, where land was converted for other uses. Interestingly, the analysis also revealed a net increase in forested area within some Central African countries, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Central African Republic.

Staver observes that while conservationists might view these findings as positive, indicating less deforestation than feared, the situation is complex. The relative stability of central African forests, she points out, is partly a consequence of violent conflicts that have stifled economic development, often at a tragic human cost.

The study's co-authors include Yale's Mart Jarzyna. Funding was provided by the National Science Foundation, the Seessel Fund, and the Yale Climate and Energy Institute.

Image copyright UTC Image caption University Technical College in Newhaven opened less than three years ago
A college which said it would shut after not attracting enough students has been rated "inadequate" by Ofsted.
University Technical College (UTC) in Newhaven, East Sussex, said on Monday it would stay open until July 2019 to allow current students to complete their courses.
Ofsted inspectors said many students were disappointed they had not received the education they had expected.
UTC acting principal Lisa Jepson said she accepted the report's findings.
"We are very disappointed by this outcome... and are committed to implementing the recommendations contained in their report for the students that remain with us until the UTC closes," she said.
The college opened in September 2015 for students aged 14 to 18 interested in science, technology, engineering, maths and computing.
College principal Adanma Umunna left suddenly a few weeks ago after being brought in after the first year by the Aldridge Foundation, one of the organisations involved in running UTC.
'Broken promises'
Ofsted found UTC to be inadequate in all areas, including leadership, quality of teaching, and outcomes for pupils.
Inspectors who visited the college found "too many promises had been broken too often" and teaching and leadership was ineffective.
Pupils felt "inadequately prepared" for exams, while those most able were not challenged enough.
The report also identified other problems, including frequent bullying, some of which was racial.
Ofsted visited UTC in May, in what was its first inspection.
On Monday, governors told parents, staff and students that the college had not been able "to recruit enough students to become financially stable and to deliver fully on its educational vision".
Children due to join this September will be offered alternative places.
rewrite:
A University Technical College in Newhaven, East Sussex, has been judged as failing across all measures by the education regulator Ofsted. The institution, which caters to pupils aged 14 to 18 with a focus on STEM subjects, had already announced plans to cease operations due to low enrollment. It will now remain open only until July 2019 to allow existing students to finish their programs.

Inspectors concluded the college was deficient in every category assessed, such as management, instructional quality, and student results. The report stated that leadership and teaching were largely unsuccessful, leaving many learners feeling let down by an education that did not meet their expectations. Promises made to pupils were frequently not honored. Additionally, students reported feeling ill-equipped for examinations, with the highest achievers not being sufficiently stretched. Further issues involved regular incidents of bullying, some motivated by racism.

The acting principal acknowledged the findings and pledged to enact the inspectorate's suggestions for the remaining pupils. The college’s original principal departed abruptly recently, having been appointed after its inaugural year by one of the sponsoring groups. This inspection in May was the first the college had undergone since opening in September 2015.

The governing body informed parents, staff, and students that the school could not attract sufficient numbers to achieve financial viability or fully realize its academic goals. Prospective pupils set to begin this autumn will be provided with placements elsewhere.

RALEIGH, N.C. (AP) - Federal wildlife officials say the only wild population of endangered red wolves is unsustainable and could be wiped out within years.
The prediction comes in a five-year review of the status of the species released Tuesday by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The report says only about 40 wolves remain in the wild in North Carolina, down from a peak of nearly 120 a decade ago. Another 230 wolves live in captivity.
The main purpose of the report was to evaluate the wolves' endangered status, which it says should be maintained. More detailed recommendations for conservation efforts will come in a separate document.
Environmentalists contend the decline is due to neglect by federal officials who have halted releases of captive-born wolves and other actions that bolstered the wild population.
rewrite:
A photograph from June 13, 2017, shows a seven-week-old red wolf pup under the watchful gaze of its parents at Durham, North Carolina's Museum of Life and Science. According to U.S. federal wildlife authorities, the sole remaining wild group of these endangered animals is no longer viable and faces potential extinction in the coming years. This assessment was detailed in a species status review, conducted every five years and made public on April 24, 2018, by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The findings indicate that merely 40 red wolves are estimated to survive in their natural habitat within North Carolina, a drastic reduction from roughly 120 individuals recorded ten years prior. An additional 230 wolves are housed in captive breeding facilities.

The principal aim of this evaluation was to analyze the continued necessity of the wolves' classification under the Endangered Species Act, a designation the report confirms remains essential. More specific proposals for recovery initiatives are slated to be outlined in a subsequent plan.

Conservation groups argue that this steep population drop results from inaction by the federal agency. They assert that the decline has been accelerated by the suspension of key management strategies, including the introduction of wolves bred in captivity into the wild and other supportive measures that previously helped sustain the free-roaming population.

Ask five basketball experts to rank the best players in the NBA and you’ll get five different lists. But, every one of those lists would include Kawhi Leonard somewhere in the top-five.
Unless you ask Penny Hardaway for his top-five, apparently. The former NBA point guard dropped a fire take over the weekend, and by “fire” I mean “god awful.” Take it away Penny…
Penny with some shots on Kawhi. pic.twitter.com/tSa7Yg93lo — ClutchPoints (@ClutchPointsApp) August 13, 2017
“He’s a good player.” Yeah, that’s an understatement. The best perimeter defender in the league can also give you 25 points a game on 48.5% shooting, but he’s merely “good.”
Leonard’s play on both ends of the court is great and all, but we’re gonna need to see him in more commercials talking to puppets before we anoint him. Same goes for Tim Duncan and Bill Russell. Sure, their 16 combined rings are impressive but have they ever appeared with Lil Yachty in a Sprite commercial? I don’t think so. #NotMySuperstars.
Seriously, though, this is a terrible take. There have always been (and will always be) low-profile superstars in sports. Barry Sanders was undoubtedly a superstar and rarely talked to the media or starred in commercials. Mike Trout is the best baseball player on the planet and is barely recognizable to casual sports fans.
In a league full of stars, Leonard manages to stand out. He doesn’t need a big social media presence or to appear in commercials to do so. His game does that for him. Leonard will never be a crossover star, but he is certainly a “superstar player,” and has been for at least two seasons now.
Now, let’s forget Hardaway ever let this nonsense come out of his mouth and just enjoy some of his highlights.
Much better.
rewrite:
If you were to request a ranking of the NBA's top talents from five different analysts, you would likely receive five distinct sets of names. However, Kawhi Leonard would almost certainly appear among the elite few on every single one.

That is, unless you happened to ask former NBA guard Penny Hardaway. Over the weekend, he shared a particularly scorching—and frankly, misguided—opinion on the matter. His social media post said it all.

His assessment? “He’s a good player.” This is a staggering understatement. Leonard, widely regarded as the league’s premier perimeter defender, also consistently scores around 25 points per game with remarkable efficiency. To label him merely “good” is to miss the mark entirely.

While his two-way dominance is undeniable, perhaps we should withhold true superstar status until he features in more advertisements with puppets. By that same logic, legends like Tim Duncan and Bill Russell fall short—despite their collective 16 championships, did they ever share screen time with a rapper in a soda commercial? The answer is no, thus apparently disqualifying them.

In all seriousness, this perspective is flawed. Sports have always had iconic figures who shun the spotlight. Barry Sanders was a transcendent football star who avoided media and endorsements. In baseball, Mike Trout is arguably the greatest active player, yet he remains unfamiliar to many casual observers.

Within a league overflowing with talent, Leonard distinguishes himself through performance alone. He doesn’t require a vibrant social media persona or a portfolio of commercials; his on-court abilities speak volumes. He may never become a mainstream celebrity, but he has undoubtedly been a superstar on the basketball court for several years now.

Let’s now dismiss Hardaway’s comments as the oddity they are and instead appreciate some of his own memorable plays from his playing days. That’s a far more worthwhile endeavor.

Chief Justice Wayne Martin has given a bleak synopsis of the life of a prisoner in WA, saying those behind bars learn little more inside than “how to improve their criminal skills before being released back into the community”.
Justice Martin is retiring after more than a decade as WA’s lead jurist. His replacement is expected to be named this month.
In one of his last speeches, to an audience at the University of WA, Justice Martin admitted during his time at the head of the WA bench, little had changed in terms of outcomes for those who ended up in prison — particularly indigenous prisoners.
“To put it bluntly, for many Australian prisoners all that happens while they are in prison is they get a little older, spend time with other offenders and perhaps improve their criminal skills before being released back into the community,” he said.
In an address to launch the idea of a new-style justice centre in WA, Justice Martin had a swipe at politicians he said engaged in pre-election “law-and-order auctions”, outbidding each other in a punitive approach to crime — which in turn led to chronically overcrowded jails.
“A purely punitive response does nothing whatever to address or mitigate (crime),” Justice Martin said.
“The regular law and order auctions ... and increasingly punitive policies have caused Australia’s prison population to grow at a much faster rate than reported crime.
“That leaves me pondering aloud as to why Australia's legislators persist with increasingly punitive policies and laws. Clearly we need a new approach.”
Figures released last month by the Australian Bureau of Statistics revealed that apart from the Northern Territory, WA has the highest number of prisoners per population in the country: 342 per 100,000 adult population.
The imprisonment rate among WA’s indigenous population is by far the highest in Australia, approaching twice the national average.
Justice Martin said the incarceration percentage was now “comparable to the highest rates of disadvantage by race in any justice system in the world”.
He said if the notion of a community justice centre similar to the one running in Victoria was to take off in WA, indigenous leaders needed to be intimately involved.
“It has been said many times that those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it,” Justice Martin said.
rewrite:
In a sobering assessment, Western Australia’s outgoing Chief Justice Wayne Martin has portrayed prison life as offering scant rehabilitation, with inmates often merely refining illicit abilities before returning to society. Justice Martin, who is stepping down after over ten years as the state’s top judicial officer, anticipates his successor will be appointed shortly.

During a recent lecture at the University of Western Australia, among his final public addresses, he conceded that throughout his tenure there has been minimal progress in improving results for incarcerated individuals—most notably for Aboriginal prisoners. He stated plainly that for numerous Australian inmates, prison merely advances their age, exposes them to fellow criminals, and potentially hones their unlawful talents, after which they are returned to the outside world.

Speaking at an event to propose a novel kind of justice centre for WA, Justice Martin criticised political figures for what he termed pre-election “law-and-order auctions,” where parties compete to adopt harsher stances on crime. This trend, he argued, results in severely overcrowded prisons. He emphasised that a solely punitive reaction fails entirely to confront or lessen criminal activity. The recurring auctions and ever-stricter policies have driven Australia’s prisoner numbers to climb far more rapidly than recorded offences, he noted. This reality prompts him to question openly why Australian lawmakers continue to enforce increasingly severe policies and statutes, asserting the clear necessity for a fresh direction.

Recent Australian Bureau of Statistics data show that, excluding the Northern Territory, Western Australia incarcerates more people per capita than any other jurisdiction, with 342 prisoners per 100,000 adults. The rate for Indigenous residents in WA is the nation’s highest by a wide margin, nearly double the national figure. Justice Martin observed that this level of imprisonment is now “similar to the worst racial disparities found in any global justice system.”

He affirmed that for a community justice centre model, akin to one operating in Victoria, to succeed in Western Australia, Indigenous representatives must play a central and engaged role. Quoting a well-known adage, Justice Martin reminded the audience that failing to heed the lessons of history ensures its repetition.

Beluga whales Qila and Aurora fell ill and died at the Vancouver Aquarium in November 2016 but their DNA will contribute to efforts to preserve this species at risk. Researchers say they have collected enough DNA samples from the mother and daughter whales to sequence the complete beluga genome. That should help scientists understand how belugas are faring in an environment that is rapidly changing.
The researchers found that neither bacteria nor viruses were responsible for the fatalities, but rather they were overcome by a toxin. They have not been able to identify exactly which one.
Qila spent almost three decades at the Vancouver Aquarium before she and her daughter died from an unidentified toxin in 2016. © Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press/file
Genome will provide ‘many tools’
Researchers think they have mapped one of the most complete mammalian genomes and that it will provide a baseline and “many tools” to study beluga whales.
A genome is the description for the entire DNA in a living organism and determines its characteristics, inherited traits, susceptibilities and it provides a window on its evolution. Researchers say mapping “can aid in identifying conservation measures for recovery, management, and protection of a species.”
The study published in the scientific journal Genes.
rewrite:
In November 2016, two beluga whales named Qila and Aurora passed away at the Vancouver Aquarium. Despite this loss, their genetic material will now support initiatives to protect this vulnerable species. Scientists report gathering sufficient DNA from the mother and daughter pair to assemble the full genetic blueprint of the beluga. This achievement is expected to aid researchers in assessing how these whales are coping with swift environmental shifts.

Investigations revealed that the deaths were not caused by an infection, but by a poisonous substance. The precise nature of this toxin remains unknown. Qila had resided at the aquarium for nearly thirty years prior to the incident.

Experts believe they have produced one of the most comprehensive genetic maps for any mammal, which will establish a reference point and offer diverse methods for examining beluga whales. A genome encompasses all the hereditary information in an organism, governing its features, inherited qualities, vulnerabilities, and evolutionary history. Scientists state that such detailed mapping can help pinpoint strategies for the revival, stewardship, and safeguarding of a species. These findings were released in the academic publication *Genes*.

Sensitive patient medical records compiled by possibly thousands of doctors may have been compromised, according to data security researcher KrebsonSecurity.
Krebs says it recently notified Kansas-based MEDantex, a medical transcription service, to a security issue with an online portal that was apparently leaking medical records onto the internet that should have been password protected. The portal has since been shut down.
"What’s more," Krebs reports, "numerous online tools intended for use by MEDantex employees were exposed to anyone with a Web browser, including pages that allowed visitors to add or delete users, and to search for patient records by physician or patient name. No authentication was required to access any of these pages."
A check of MEDantex's website includes a client list of multiple medical organizations across the country from San Francisco to New York, and from New Jersey to Florida.
The company's website lists Montgomery, Alabama's Jackson Hospital among its clients, but when contacted by WSFA 12 News, MEDantex CEO Sreeram Pydah said Jackson has not been a client since sometime between 2003 and 2005. He added that he doesn't believe Jackson records are on the impacted server and called it a "very low chance" any of Jackson's records were impacted.
When reached for comment, Jackson Hospital spokeswoman Mia Mothershed said MEDantex is investigating the breach "and [has] not identified the scope of information compromised." She added that Jackson Hospital "has not been identified among the companies whose information was exposed. If confirmation is received we will take appropriate action."
Krebs said the number of exposed records was unclear, but one accessible directory alphabetized more than 2,300 doctors by their last name with access to downloadable records. While most records appeared recent, some dated back to at least 2007, Krebs stated.
So what could the data be used for? Krebs indicates one possibility.
"Several MEDantex portal pages left exposed to the Web suggest that the company recently was the victim of WhiteRose," Krebs wrote, "a strain of ransomware that encrypts a victim’s files unless and until a ransom demand is paid."
Pydah tells WSFA 12 News security experts are investigating what he called a ransomware attack but don't yet know the extent or who was affected. He said it could take weeks to get more information.
Copyright 2018 WSFA 12 News. All rights reserved.
rewrite:
A potential data breach may have exposed confidential medical information belonging to patients from numerous physicians, as detailed by cybersecurity investigator KrebsonSecurity. The report indicates that MEDantex, a transcription provider located in Kansas, was alerted to a vulnerability in one of its web platforms. This system was inadvertently making protected health documents accessible online without the necessary security credentials. Following this discovery, the portal was taken offline.

Krebs further notes that several internal web applications for MEDantex staff were publicly available, requiring no login. These interfaces permitted unrestricted actions such as registering or removing user accounts, as well as querying patient files by either doctor or patient name. A review of the firm's official site shows a portfolio of healthcare clients spanning various states, from California to New York and from New Jersey to Florida.

Although Jackson Hospital in Montgomery, Alabama, appears on the client roster, MEDantex's chief executive, Sreeram Pydah, clarified to WSFA 12 News that the hospital has not been a client since approximately the mid-2000s. He expressed doubt that any Jackson Hospital records were stored on the affected server, characterizing the likelihood of exposure as minimal. When contacted, Mia Mothershed, a representative for Jackson Hospital, stated that MEDantex is currently assessing the incident and has not yet determined the full range of potentially compromised data. She confirmed that Jackson Hospital has not been listed among entities with verified exposure but pledged to act accordingly if that status changes.

The exact volume of leaked records remains uncertain, according to Krebs. However, one openly accessible file directory catalogued over 2,300 physicians alphabetically, each associated with patient records available for download. While many documents seemed current, some were traced back to 2007 or earlier.

Regarding potential misuse of the data, Krebs points to one concerning scenario. Evidence from the exposed portal implies that MEDantex may have recently fallen prey to WhiteRose, a type of ransomware that locks files until a payment is made. Pydah informed WSFA 12 News that specialists are examining what he described as a ransomware incident, but the full scope and impacted parties are still unknown. He estimated that gathering clearer details could require several weeks.

Former state environmental agency head and Charleston lawyer Michael Callaghan is collaborating with Prosecuting Attorney Larry Harrah to address contamination in Fayette County through a dedicated financial account.

Their approach involves identifying those liable, along with their insurers, for polluting the region, including the disposal of hazardous PCBs in Minden. Any settlements secured from these insurers would be deposited into a trust specifically designated for remediation efforts.

Brandon Richardson, who leads the environmental organization Headwaters Defense, expressed skepticism in an interview with WOAY. He worries the funds may not ultimately support cleanup, noting that affected residents will likely seek compensation from the same entities. Richardson fears this could create conflict and that county management of the money might not be optimal.

Given Fayette County's status as a tourist destination, there is strong local interest in ensuring the area is cleansed of pollutants. Harrah emphasized to the Register Herald that the area's popularity with visitors makes this initiative particularly urgent.

By Scott T. Sterling
Pop singer Rachel Platten is set to return with a new album, Waves, which will be released on Oct. 27.
Related: Rachel Platten Debuts New Single ‘Broken Glass’
“I loved making this album, I’ve never felt so free creatively,” Platten revealed in a press statement. “I wrote all of these songs without getting in the way, and I just let whatever needed to come through me just come. I worked out a lot of heavy stuff on some of the songs and cried on my piano at 3 a.m. some nights, but I also woke up some days and jumped into the ocean and felt amazing and just wanted to write songs I could dance to. This album is raw and it’s emotional, but it’s also fun and sweet and it’s real. It’s honestly just all of me and I am so damn proud of it.”
Among the producers on Waves include OneRepublic’s Ryan Tedder and Stargate.

"Can you imagine him having a kid at this age?" she asked, shaking her head.
When she's away and Christer looks after their two puppies on his own, he usually brings them here and tells me how exhausting they are. It is difficult for me to imagine anything more unlikely than Christopher having a child when I did. Discovering he can't count made me even more nervous.
"I could tell him in exquisite detail all about the night he was born … 26 years ago," I told Pam. "It was a lovely Halloween night until he announced his imminent arrival two weeks early. I recall every excruciating minute of his two-hour delivery, all aided and abetted by the fact they wouldn't give me any drugs."
I didn't get any drugs with the next kid, either, something I am apparently still bitter about. Like my mother before me, when we deliver, the doctor needs a catcher's mitt.
"I had to get his driver's licence out to prove to him that he was 26," she laughed.
I recalled those posters they have up in the LCBO that ask, "do I look 25?" and thought of Christopher looking in the mirror and asking himself a similar question.
We don't really celebrate birthdays around here, mostly based on my philosophy that unless your birthday ends in a zero or you count your age in "and a halfs," they matter little. One rolls into the next and before you know it, you're 26. Or 27. Or 54.
This led me to realize that it was perhaps my fault that my son didn't know how old he was. I looked at his sad text, a grown man uncertain of his actual age for two solid months. I texted back the only thing that would express my remorse.
"You're an idiot."

“Can you picture him raising a child right now?” she wondered with a dismissive shake of her head. Whenever she’s out and Christer is solely responsible for their two young dogs, he often brings them over and complains about how draining they are. For me, it’s nearly impossible to conceive of Christopher becoming a parent at the same stage I once did. Learning that he struggles with basic numbers only heightened my anxiety.

I mentioned to Pam, “I could describe every minute of the evening he arrived … twenty-six years back.” It was a pleasant Halloween night until he decided to come ahead of schedule by two weeks. I remember each painful moment of that two-hour labor, made worse because I wasn’t allowed any pain relief.”

I didn’t receive medication during my next delivery either—a fact that clearly still bothers me. Much like my mother in her time, when my children are born, the doctor ought to be equipped with a catcher’s mitt.

She chuckled as she said, “I actually had to show him his own driver’s license to convince him he was twenty-six.”

That brought to mind the signs posted in liquor stores questioning, “Do I appear 25?” I imagined Christopher examining his reflection and pondering something along those lines.

Birthdays aren’t a big occasion in our household, largely due to my belief that unless it’s a milestone ending in zero or you’re still measuring your age in half-years, they hardly seem significant. One year blends into another, and suddenly you’re twenty-six. Or twenty-seven. Or fifty-four.

It dawned on me that I might be to blame for my son not knowing his own age. I read his dejected message—a full-grown man who had been unsure of his true age for two entire months. I replied with the only words that could convey my regret: “You’re an idiot.”
